title: Organ-Specific Autoantibodies: Coeliac Serology and AMA in PBC
summary: Order and interpret coeliac serology correctly — IgA anti-TG2 with total IgA on a gluten diet, IgG tests in IgA deficiency, HLA-DQ2/8 to rule out — and apply AMA within the two-of-three criteria for primary biliary cholangitis.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 55 Hits 1, 2, 7 and 10 and Trap 1 (first lesson for Ch. 55). Checked against the ESsCD 2025 adult guideline (Part 1) and APASL 2022 PBC guidance. Discrepancies: the reviewer presents anti-EMA as the confirmation test; ESsCD 2025 no longer recommends routine IgA-EMA confirmation in adults (register rv-ema-confirm). The reviewer’s “1–3 months on gluten” is close to ESsCD’s ≥ 3 g/day for 6 weeks. Not taught as fact: tTG 94%/97%, DQ2 ~90%/DQ8 ~5%, AMA ≥ 1:40 threshold and titre–severity non-correlation, ALP ≥ 1.5 × ULN for > 24 weeks, and the other Ch. 55 topics (PLA2R, lupus nephritis IF, blistering diseases, AIH scores, MG, IAA, PSC, C3G, Graves, pernicious anaemia).

objectives: Order first-line coeliac serology with its two preconditions and choose IgG-based tests in IgA deficiency.
Explain the predictive values of HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing and the gluten-challenge approach.
Apply the two-of-three criteria for primary biliary cholangitis, including the role of AMA.

scenes.title: A negative screen that proves nothing
scenes.altText: Two invented requests. (1) A 34-year-old with iron-deficiency anaemia and bloating has been on a self-started gluten-free diet for 3 months; IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-TG2) is NEGATIVE; total IgA was not measured. (2) A 55-year-old woman has raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and GGT with a normal bile-duct scan; anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is POSITIVE. Question token: “Does the first result rule out coeliac disease — and what does the second need?”

cues.text: A 34-year-old with anaemia and bloating has a negative IgA anti-transglutaminase test, but has avoided gluten for three months, and total IgA was never checked.
A 55-year-old woman has raised ALP and GGT, a normal bile-duct scan, and a positive anti-mitochondrial antibody.
Does the first result rule out coeliac disease? And what does the second patient need for a diagnosis?

props.label: Coeliac ruled out? What does PBC need?

scenes.title: The first-line coeliac test and its two conditions
scenes.altText: Recommendation card (ESsCD 2025, adults): IgA anti-TG2 as a single test for initial testing at any age; measure TOTAL IgA concurrently to exclude IgA deficiency; perform testing while the patient is on a GLUTEN-CONTAINING diet; use validated high-performance assays. Schematic: a “gauge” (IgA anti-TG2) that only reads correctly when the “tank” (total IgA) is not empty and the “fuel” (dietary gluten) is flowing.

cues.text: For coeliac disease, the European guideline recommends one first test at any age: IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase.
But it comes with two conditions. First, measure total IgA at the same time, because an IgA test cannot be positive in someone who makes no IgA.
Second, the patient must be eating gluten. The antibodies are driven by gluten, so a gluten-free diet can make the test falsely negative.
And the laboratory should use a validated, high-performance assay.

scenes.title: When the conditions fail
scenes.altText: IgA-deficiency card (ESsCD 2025): with confirmed total IgA deficiency, use IgG-based assays (IgG anti-TG2 or IgG anti-deamidated gluten peptide, DGP); because of their lower sensitivity, a NEGATIVE IgG result does not exclude coeliac disease. Gluten card (ESsCD 2025): for a patient already gluten-free, confirm HLA-DQ2/DQ8 first (a negative result rules out coeliac disease), then a gluten challenge of at least 3 g/day for 6 weeks before testing. HLA card (ESsCD 2025): HLA-DQ2/8 typing has a POOR positive predictive value but a HIGH negative predictive value; it is not used routinely for initial diagnosis, only when the diagnosis is uncertain.

cues.text: If total IgA is absent, IgA-based tests are useless. Switch to IgG-based tests: IgG anti-transglutaminase or IgG anti-deamidated gluten peptide. They are less sensitive, so a negative still does not exclude coeliac disease.

If the patient has already stopped gluten, check HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 first. If both are absent, coeliac disease is ruled out. If present, a gluten challenge of at least 3 grams a day for 6 weeks comes before testing.
HLA typing works only one way. Many healthy people carry DQ2 or DQ8, so a positive result proves little, but a negative result makes coeliac disease very unlikely.
That is why HLA typing is kept for uncertain cases, not used as a first test.

props.title: IgA deficiency
lines: Use IgG anti-TG2 or IgG anti-DGP

props.label: Not a first test — for uncertain cases

scenes.title: Confirming coeliac disease and primary biliary cholangitis
scenes.altText: Confirmation card (ESsCD 2025, adults): routine IgA anti-endomysium (EMA) for confirmation is NO LONGER recommended; a no-biopsy diagnosis is conditionally recommended for adults < 45 years with IgA anti-TG2 ≥ 10 × ULN confirmed on a second blood sample; otherwise duodenal biopsy. PBC card (APASL 2022): AMA — especially AMA-M2, which targets the 2-oxo-acid dehydrogenase complexes (e.g. PDC-E2) of the inner mitochondrial membrane — has sensitivity and specificity > 90–95%. PBC is diagnosed when 2 or more of 3 criteria are met: biochemical cholestasis (mainly ALP and GGT) with extrahepatic obstruction excluded by imaging; AMA (or PBC-specific ANA); compatible histology. About 5% of PBC is AMA-negative; anti-gp210 and anti-sp100 are highly specific (> 95%) but insensitive (15–40%). Hook answers: Patient 1 — not ruled out (measure total IgA; HLA then gluten challenge); Patient 2 — cholestasis + AMA = 2 of 3 criteria.

cues.text: In adults, the 2025 guideline no longer recommends routine endomysial antibody testing for confirmation. A biopsy is usually still needed.
The exception: adults under 45 with IgA anti-transglutaminase at least ten times the upper limit, confirmed on a second sample, may be diagnosed without biopsy.

Primary biliary cholangitis has its own antibody: anti-mitochondrial antibody, especially AMA-M2, over 90 percent sensitive and specific. The diagnosis needs two of three criteria: cholestasis with obstruction excluded, AMA, and compatible histology.
So patient 1 is not ruled out: check total IgA, then HLA and a gluten challenge. Patient 2 already meets two of three criteria for primary biliary cholangitis.

props.label: Hook: CeD not excluded · PBC criteria met (2 of 3)

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A negative IgA anti-TG2 on a gluten-free diet excludes coeliac disease” (✓ test on a gluten-containing diet; if already gluten-free, HLA then gluten challenge ≥ 3 g/day × 6 weeks); “IgA anti-TG2 alone is enough” (✓ measure total IgA — in IgA deficiency use IgG anti-TG2/DGP); “A positive HLA-DQ2 confirms coeliac disease” (✓ poor PPV — its value is a negative result).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative IgA anti-transglutaminase on a gluten-free diet excludes coeliac disease. No: test while eating gluten, or use HLA typing and a gluten challenge.
Trap two: the IgA test alone is enough. No: always measure total IgA. In IgA deficiency, switch to IgG-based tests.
Trap three: a positive HLA-DQ2 confirms coeliac disease. No: many healthy people carry it. HLA typing is useful when it is negative.

props.title: ✗ “Negative on a gluten-free diet = no CeD.”
✗ “HLA-DQ2+ confirms CeD.”
lines: ✓ Poor PPV — negative is what helps

scenes.title: Gauge, tank and fuel
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Don’t trust the tTG GAUGE until you’ve checked the IgA TANK and the gluten FUEL. HLA is the ignition key: no key (negative) means the car can’t run; having a key doesn’t mean it’s moving.” Tokens: tTG = gauge · total IgA = tank · gluten = fuel · HLA = key. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: do not trust the transglutaminase gauge until you have checked the IgA tank and the gluten fuel. HLA is the ignition key: no key means coeliac disease cannot run; having a key does not mean it is running.

Where it breaks: seronegative coeliac disease exists even with a full tank and fuel; a no-biopsy diagnosis applies only to selected adults; and some primary biliary cholangitis is AMA-negative, needing other antibodies or histology.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: No-biopsy route only for selected adults

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Coeliac: IgA anti-TG2 + total IgA, on gluten · IgA-deficient → IgG anti-TG2/DGP · HLA-DQ2/8 high NPV · routine EMA no longer needed (ESsCD 2025)”, “PBC: 2 of 3 — cholestasis (obstruction excluded), AMA-M2, histology”.

cues.text: An IgA anti-transglutaminase result means something only when total IgA is adequate and the patient is eating gluten, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 is useful mainly to rule coeliac disease out, and primary biliary cholangitis is diagnosed by two of three criteria including AMA.

props.label: CeD: IgA anti-TG2 + total IgA, on gluten · IgA-def → IgG · HLA high NPV

explanation.what: Plain language: coeliac blood tests look for IgA antibodies made in response to gluten, so they fail if someone makes no IgA or has stopped eating gluten; a gene test can rule coeliac disease out but not in. In primary biliary cholangitis, an antibody against mitochondria plus liver tests usually make the diagnosis. Scientific terms: tissue transglutaminase (TG2), total IgA, IgA deficiency, deamidated gluten peptide (DGP), endomysial antibody (EMA), HLA-DQ2/DQ8, positive and negative predictive value, gluten challenge, anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA-M2), PDC-E2, cholestasis, anti-gp210, anti-sp100.
explanation.why: Anti-TG2 IgA is produced while gluten drives the immune response, so it needs both IgA production and gluten exposure. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 is necessary but common, giving a high NPV and poor PPV. AMA targets mitochondrial 2-oxo-acid dehydrogenase complexes and is highly specific for PBC.
explanation.measure: IgA anti-TG2 + total IgA on a gluten-containing diet; IgG anti-TG2/DGP in IgA deficiency; HLA then ≥ 3 g/day gluten × 6 weeks if already gluten-free; adults < 45 with anti-TG2 ≥ 10 × ULN on two samples may skip biopsy (ESsCD 2025). PBC: 2 of 3 — cholestasis with obstruction excluded, AMA (or PBC-specific ANA), histology (APASL 2022).
explanation.differs: IgA anti-TG2 (first line) vs IgG anti-TG2/DGP (IgA deficiency, lower sensitivity); HLA positive (proves little) vs HLA negative (rules out); AMA-positive PBC vs AMA-negative PBC (~5%; anti-gp210/sp100).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: add total IgA to a coeliac screen, pick IgG-DGP in IgA deficiency, recognize a false-negative screen on a gluten-free diet, use HLA to exclude, and apply PBC criteria.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected coeliac disease has undetectable total IgA. Which test should be used?

options.text: IgG anti-TG2 or IgG anti-deamidated gluten peptide
options.rationale: Correct. In confirmed IgA deficiency, IgG-based assays are used; a negative does not exclude disease.
Incorrect. An IgA test cannot become positive without IgA.
Incorrect. HLA cannot confirm coeliac disease; it can only help exclude it.

questions.stem: A patient who has been gluten-free for a year wants to know if they have coeliac disease. HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 are both negative. What is the conclusion?

options.text: Coeliac disease is effectively ruled out; no gluten challenge is needed
options.rationale: Correct. HLA-DQ2/8 typing has a high negative predictive value.

options.text: Start a gluten challenge of 3 g/day for 6 weeks
options.rationale: Incorrect. A challenge is for HLA-positive patients; negative HLA rules out coeliac disease.
Incorrect. Negative HLA argues strongly against it.

options.text: Test IgA anti-TG2 while still gluten-free
options.rationale: Incorrect. Serology on a gluten-free diet can be falsely negative and adds little here.

questions.stem: A woman has raised ALP and GGT, a normal bile-duct scan and a positive AMA-M2. Liver biopsy has not been done. Under APASL guidance, can PBC be diagnosed?

options.text: Yes — cholestasis with obstruction excluded plus AMA meets 2 of 3 criteria
options.rationale: Correct. Two or more of the three criteria establish the diagnosis.
Incorrect. Histology is one of three criteria, not mandatory.

options.text: No — AMA alone is never useful
options.rationale: Incorrect. AMA-M2 is a diagnostic hallmark with > 90–95% sensitivity and specificity.

options.text: Only if anti-gp210 is also positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. gp210/sp100 help mainly in AMA-negative PBC.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer presents anti-endomysial antibody as the confirmation test (“nearly 100% specific for confirmation”). The ESsCD 2025 adult guideline states that routine IgA-EMA serology is no longer recommended for confirmation; adults are confirmed by biopsy or, in selected cases, by high-titre anti-TG2 on two samples.
